en: That would not end in five or six days.
When Chürök's desire comes,
She has a husband she keeps concealed.
I know Chürök's origin,
The turmoil that has come to an end.
Alas, my Kozho, hear my words!
There is a flaw in what you say:
That man is Aychürök's husband.
There is a son left by Manas.
Will he submit to your violence?
Will he give us his wife?
One of my ears has heard this:
When Semetey was born,
He consumed the Russians' feast.
If he lived and grew,
They said he would shatter the Oirats.
He consumed the Chinese feast;
If this boy remained alive,
They said he would shatter the age.
He has a tale that does not end—
In a tumultuous land she has a hero.
Alas, Kozho, hear my words,
You pass on rumbling and raging.
Raging onward, one day
You will reach my very end with me.
If you rage with brute force,
You will dig a deep grave,
You will make my sorrow boil.
Before my eyes you will show
A marvel no man has seen.
You will have us wait on the yellow steppe,
And you will make us contend
With the son Manas left behind.
Why do you covet, Chynkozho,
Akun's daughter Churek?
My khan Kozho, you mean to meddle
In turmoil from which there is no recovery.
You had the goats for provisions slaughtered,
Withered Kozho, may you come to no good,
You are about to make us suffer punishment.
You have brought Afghanistan's city down upon us,
You are about to lay upon my head
A calamity no man would cause.
You have thrown the exhausted people into alarm,
You mean to lodge the guest overnight,
Ruined Kozho, thundering on,
You are making me tell this tale.
You are a wretched Kozho,
Does she know what you have said?
Akun's daughter Aychurek—
If we implore her, will she marry us?
Will God consent to force?
She is to be Manas's daughter-in-law—
Will Akun Khan give her to us?
Akun Khan's daughter Aychurek
Strokes the flanks of her horse,
The luckless one, rich in magic,
Throughout the whole wide world
She flies and travels.
Hero Kozho, hear my words!
Sleeping in the night, I dreamed a dream,
I saw a dreadful, grievous deed.
I will not take your Aychurek,
I will not fall into her torment.
There is a flaw in these words of yours:
Will they give us the wife
When the son Manas left behind still lives?
When I slept at night and dreamed,
I saw an evil deed in my dream.
He rode a red-bay horse,
Its horsehair tail tied with a snap.
He had buckled on a silver belt,
A dark mark lay across his sun-bright face.
Thick-wristed and stone-hearted,
A fierce young hero filled with courage.
His sword, for my ravenous destroyer,
Was bound bare to his body without a sheath.
Like a cloud about to rain again,
He wheeled back and forth.
At the sight, my heart was torn apart,
Wrath poured from his face.
Of middle height and broad shoulders,
He was clad entirely in iron.
He roared in fury;
If seven successive hosts came,
He faced them alone and scattered them.
A demon-like boy,
He shouted the battle cry, “Manas!”
Leveling his spear,
In this manner he brought to an end
Every stratagem of your Toltoy.
Manas led countless men.
Azhybay, Bakay, and Almambet,
Valiant Chubak, and a thousand men
Charged in along my flank,
Each of them thrust a spear,
And struck me as they closed around.
My fly-like soul screamed out,
The places where the spears passed through
Remain even now,
Gushing though I do not move.
Having seen a most ill-omened dream,
I lay there, poor soul,
Suffering a most dreadful plight.
My dream in the night was an evil dream;
The edges of my ribs ache.
As though I had been stabbed while awake,
The very crown of my heart aches.
Going about to take Aychürök,
I will not remain in her torment.
Roaming among a mere handful of people,
I will not bear their sin.
This is grievous, disastrous work;
Do not give orders, Kozho, my dear friend.
There is a flaw in these words of yours:
Will he submit to your violence?
Will he give us his wife?
There is a son left by Manas.
Have you heard the news
Of the blue-maned lion Manas,
Who was born and grew mighty in Altai?
The lion Manas, the magnanimous lion,
When he reached the age of twelve,
Came saying, "I will fight,"
And the Kara Kalmyks and Manchu people,
So many Sibe and hosts of Solon,
Were slaughtered and all humiliated.
His name was heard through the ages;
Kyzyr blessed him, and he grew mighty.
Yesterday, heading toward the mountains of Altai,
Esen Khan's thousand troops,
And among those troops,
Beaded hat-buttons and coral stones,
With the lungtung khan among them,
To capture and bind Manas,
They received their khan's order.
So great a host
Had settled over the land.
His father Jakyp and Akbaltay
Had scattered all their wealth.
All the Kyrgyz of forty households
Had fled for refuge to the mountains.
Before the mighty Kara Khitai,
When they were about to overrun their villages,
Seize them all,
And slaughter them as sacrifices,
Girding a leather belt about his waist,
Against the seven divisions of Kara Khitai
He entered alone and laid hands upon them.
Poor Manas the lion,
Making his dapple-gray horse dance,
With Khan Zholoy at their head,
Drove them crawling all the way to Beijing.
The Chinese who attacked him fell;
Before the lion, Sultan Manas,
The foe he fixed his gaze upon fell.
Called "Manas the bloodthirsty Burut,"
His name became known throughout the world.
In the register of Beijing's Kökön Khan
He was inscribed.
When they heard this news,
All the countless Chinese,
Beginning with Esen Khan, grieved.
The daughter-in-law of that very Manas—
How will you take her?
If you carry on this way, Chynkozho,
You will fall into disaster.
If you seize her, Chynkozho,
Will God not strike you?
Will Semetey let her be taken
And stand watching without a quarrel?
Against the son of the Kyzyr-blessed lion,
Can anyone who attacks prosper?
Again, Kozho, hear my words!
That Manas was truly Manas,
It seems you have seen it, damn you!"
Your headstrong wildness is worst of all;
Unable to settle your quarrel,
You have come here.
Leopard Manas, the bloodthirsty lion,
When he reached the age of twelve,
Moved here
And found a home in bushy Talas,
And found the forty Kyrgyz tribes as his people.
When he came and settled in Talas,
The whole populace gave everything
To Manas, Jakyp's only son.
When Manas came to Talas,
He kept a son as a hostage.
From the khan of the Kakan people, from Beijing,
A khan named Alööke arose.
Not a soul remained to answer him back;
People died from his wrath.
Sparing none of the people from tribute,
Alööke kept exacting it.
Whoever incurred his wrath,
Alööke seized and, like a kid goat,
Cut him down.
Whoever answered him back,
He had dragged along the road,
Made a feast of him for the Dangyt,
And had him ripped apart.
In a pitch-black dungeon
Alööke kept him imprisoned.
Whoever defied him,
He cut straps from his back
And kept flogging him.
Such were Alööke's deeds:
When anyone went to Alööke,
Every person who went
Paid homage and bowed.
Alööke's deeds
To magnanimous Sultan Manas
Became clearly known.
With Khan Bakai and Manas at their head,
When they launched an assault
Against Alööke,
And heard reports from those who came,
Brave Manas went to meet him
And, they heard, burned everything down.
All his possessions were scattered;
Scorched by the fire, Alööke
Fled toward Beijing.
From where he settled, Alööke
Overran broad Kashgar.
When he reached Great Aksy
And crossed Kum-Aryk,
At the edge of broad Ak-Chiy,
Alööke posted his sentries
And made camp.
Brave Manas bore down on him
From above
And scattered all four kinds of his livestock.
He caught up with him and seized him,
And slaughtered him as a sacrifice.
Saying, “Manas slaughtered my father,”
Alööke's son Kongurbai
Came to bear a grudge
Against noble, magnanimous Manas.
Manas was such a hero:
For the mere handful of Muslims,
Magnanimous Manas the leopard
Was a fortress that protected them.
What twelve ages had never wrought,
Ruining Sultan Manas did;
In that bygone age,
Not a stick for a horse-catching pole remained.
Manas was such a hero;
His fortune was complete.
When one looked within him,
He was broader than the face of the earth.
A hero like Manas,
For the Muslim people—
The Creator would surely never grant another.
Where the racehorse Akkula had not trodden,
Nothing on earth remained whole.
